item_text: I notice when my body feels tense or keyed up.
When my responsibilities increase, I make choices that allow time for my body to recover.
When my schedule becomes demanding, I make deliberate choices that protect my recovery.
I can adjust my pace or take a useful break when my energy is dropping.
I can manage my energy across a day with several responsibilities.
When I notice something in my daily life is affecting how my body is functioning, I make a change.
I take practical steps to look after my body when I see it's not functioning well.
I can recognise when pressure is showing up in my body.
When demands build up, I notice the physical signs that pressure is affecting me.
I can maintain useful daily routines even when my schedule changes.
When my routine is disrupted, I can put a new one in place.
I can keep important personal routines going even when I have several responsibilities at once.
When I decide that a daily habit needs to change, I can take a practical first step.
I can make health-supportive choices even when it's inconvenient.
I can tell when I'm physically tired, even if I want to keep going.
When I feel keyed up or on edge, I know at least one practical way to calm my body.
I notice when my everyday habits are affecting how my body functions, and I can change them.
When my body gives me a warning sign that I am under too much pressure, I pay attention to it.
When I'm busy, I still make time to rest and recover.
When things change, I can adjust my routine instead of giving it up completely.
When I decide to make a health-related change, I can turn that decision into a practical first step.
I notice when I am using more energy than a situation requires and can slow down when needed.
I respond to important physical needs before they interfere with what I need to do.
I can notice when my emotional state is starting to change.
I can tell the difference between emotions that feel similar to me.
I can distinguish between different emotions that arise in the same situation.
I can usually identify what is contributing to an emotion I am experiencing.
I can consider more than one possible reason for an emotional reaction.
I can express what I am feeling in a way that others can understand.
I can communicate difficult feelings clearly while still taking responsibility for my own feelings.
When an emotion becomes intense, I can do something that helps me respond rather than react automatically.
I can change how I respond when an emotion is making a situation harder to handle.
I can stay with an uncomfortable feeling long enough to decide what I need to do.
I can pause before acting when I feel a strong emotional urge.
I can adjust how I deal with an emotion when my first approach is not helping.
If a way of handling my emotions is not working, I can try a different approach.
After I make a mistake, I can treat myself with understanding while still taking responsibility.
I can allow myself to enjoy positive experiences without immediately dismissing them.
I can notice and enjoy small positive moments even during a demanding period.
After a difficult emotional experience, I can gradually return to my usual functioning.
I can recognise that my emotions about the same situation can change over time.
I can choose a way of managing an emotion that fits the situation.
When I feel an uncomfortable emotion, I can notice it without immediately trying to push it away.
After a difficult emotional experience, I can notice signs that I am becoming more settled and able to function again.
I notice changes in how people are responding to me.
I can notice changes in how people are interacting with each other before I decide how to respond.
I can consider how a situation may look from another person's point of view.
When people disagree, I can identify a reason their view might make sense to them.
I feel concern for people even when their situation doesn't affect me directly.
I can feel for someone even when I'm not certain exactly what they're going through.
I can communicate what I mean clearly enough for others to understand.
I can change how I communicate when my usual way is not helping the other person understand.
I can work with others toward a shared task even when we have different preferences.
When a group I'm working with isn't coordinating well, I can suggest a different way of dividing up the work or communicating.
I can recognise when I need a boundary in a relationship or interaction.
I can maintain a personal limit even when someone pressures me to change it.
I can express what I need or prefer without putting down the other person.
I can speak up when my needs are important even if others may disagree.
When there is a disagreement, I can focus on understanding the issue and deciding what needs to happen next.
I can recognise when a disagreement needs discussion, a pause or another way of handling it.
When my actions have affected someone negatively, I can take a step to repair the relationship.
If a relationship problem is partly my responsibility, I can acknowledge my part and work toward repair.
When I need support from another person, I can ask for it.
If I cannot resolve something on my own, I can identify someone appropriate to ask for help.
I can take steps to maintain relationships that are important to me.
When I enter a new social environment, I can take steps to get to know people.
I think about how a message or post may affect another person before I send or share it.
When an online interaction becomes uncomfortable, I can decide how to handle it in the moment.
I have a reasonably clear sense of the kind of person I am.
I can explain how different parts of my life fit with my sense of who I am.
My sense of worth does not depend entirely on how well I perform.
A setback in one area does not completely determine how I judge myself.
I can recognise when different parts of my life feel difficult to fit together and think about what each part means to me.
When my roles or commitments pull me in different directions, I can work out what fits together and what does not.
I can make choices that are consistent with what I genuinely think and value, even when other people may choose differently.
I can notice when a choice reflects what I genuinely want and when it mainly reflects what I think others expect from me.
I can make important choices based on reasons that I personally accept.
I can distinguish between choices I genuinely endorse and choices I am making mainly because I feel pressured.
I can identify the principles that matter to me when I make important choices.
When I face an important choice, I can identify which values or principles are most relevant to me.
I can identify actions I can take to influence outcomes that matter to me.
When I cannot control an outcome, I can identify what I can still influence through my own actions.
I can identify activities, relationships or goals that give my life a sense of meaning.
I can connect some of my current choices with what I find personally meaningful.
I can think about how choices I make now may affect my future.
I can consider how my current priorities may affect the options available to me later.
I can make an important decision after considering what matters, what I know and what I do not know.
When I need to make a decision without knowing everything, I can use the information I have to choose a reasonable way forward.
When I want to reach an important goal, I can think of more than one possible way forward.
When a route toward an important goal closes, I can identify other routes that may still fit what I want.
I can recognise my part in an outcome without taking responsibility for things I could not control.
I can take responsibility for actions I control while recognising limits to my control over outcomes.
When my usual way of handling a difficult situation isn't working, I can try a different way of responding to it.
When new information changes what a situation requires, I can adjust how I'm thinking about it or responding to it.
I can match how I cope with a difficulty to what the situation actually needs, rather than relying on one fixed approach.
I can recognise when a coping approach that has worked before isn’t the right fit for a new situation, and adjust.
I can function reasonably well even when I don’t know how a situation will turn out.
I can make a reasonable decision even when I don’t have all the information I would like to have.
After something doesn’t go the way I hoped, I can figure out a reasonable next step.
When a setback happens, I can take some time to process it and then figure out how to move forward.
When I fail at something that matters to me, I can process it and figure out what to do next rather than shutting down.
After a significant failure, I can identify a next step rather than staying stuck in how bad it feels.
I can approach a difficult situation as something to work through rather than only as a threat to avoid.
I can take on a demanding situation by focusing on what I might be able to do about it, rather than only on what could go wrong.
After a difficult period, I can gradually get back to functioning in my day-to-day life.
Following a difficult stretch, I can rebuild my day-to-day functioning over time, even if it takes a while.
I can look back at a difficult experience and identify something useful I learned from it.
I can extract a useful lesson from a difficult experience without needing everything to have gone perfectly for it to be useful.
When something in my life changes unexpectedly, I can start adjusting to the new situation rather than resisting it.
When I can see a change coming, I can start preparing for it before it happens.
Even when I’m having a difficult thought or feeling, I can still act in ways that matter to me.
I can hold uncomfortable thoughts or feelings without letting them completely stop me from doing what matters to me.
I can bring my attention back to what I need to focus on when it starts to drift.
When I notice that my attention has moved away from an important task, I can bring it back to what I need to do.
I can keep my attention on an important task even when it takes longer than expected.
I can pause before taking an action when doing it immediately could interfere with an important task.
I can resist doing something immediately when waiting would help me complete an important task.
I can stop myself from responding immediately when a situation requires a more considered response.
I use reminders, notes or lists to keep track of what I need to do.
When a task has several parts, I use a method like a checklist or notes to keep track of what's needed.
I keep track of task details using tools such as lists, reminders or notes, rather than relying only on memory.
When an important task needs to be done, I can take a first step without waiting to feel fully ready.
When an important task needs attention, I can begin even when I would rather be doing something else.
When I have been putting off an important responsibility, I can take a concrete first step toward doing it.
I can break an important task into steps that help me move it forward.
When a task feels large, I can divide it into smaller steps.
For a complex task, I can identify the main steps and an order in which to approach them.
I can organise the information or tasks I need so that I can use them when required.
I can keep track of what needs to be done when I have several responsibilities at the same time.
I can organise important responsibilities in a way that helps me follow through on them.
I can judge how well I understand something and recognise when my understanding may be incomplete.
I can tell when I understand something well enough and when I need to learn more.
I can recognise when my understanding of a topic is incomplete before relying on it.
I can choose a learning approach that fits what I am trying to learn.
I can choose different ways of studying depending on what I need to learn.
I can change my learning approach when the demands of a task require a different strategy.
While working, I can notice when I have misunderstood something or made an error that needs attention.
I can check my progress during an important task and recognise when I need to change what I am doing.
I can check my progress during important work and adjust if I am not moving toward the intended result.
I can evaluate useful feedback and apply what is relevant to improve my work.
When feedback does not seem useful for the task, I can consider it without automatically changing what I am doing.
I can consider feedback and decide what change, if any, would improve my approach.
When I lack information needed for an important task, I can identify the gap and seek an appropriate source.
When I do not understand something important, I can identify what I need to find out next.
When my knowledge is insufficient for an important responsibility, I can identify useful sources or information to close the gap.
When I need to learn something, I can take independent steps to move my learning forward.
I can take some steps to learn something on my own after I know what I need to understand.
I can organise my own learning when a responsibility requires me to develop knowledge or skill independently.
When reliable evidence shows that my understanding may be wrong, I can reconsider my view.
If I find evidence that challenges what I think, I can consider whether I need to change my understanding.
When credible information challenges my view, I can examine it before deciding whether my view needs to change.
I can turn an intended outcome into a clear goal that guides what I do next.
When I want to achieve something, I can make the goal clear enough to know what I am trying to do.
I can define an important goal clearly enough to guide what I do next.
When progress toward an important goal is slow, I can continue working while considering whether my approach needs to change.
When an important goal becomes difficult, I can keep working toward it when the goal is still worth pursuing.
I can sustain effort toward an important goal while checking whether it still makes sense to pursue it.
I can compare my progress with what I intended to achieve and decide what needs to change.
I can check how my progress compares with what I planned and decide what to change.
I can review progress toward an important goal and identify whether my next action needs to change.
I focus on improving my understanding or ability, not only on demonstrating that I can already do something well.
When learning something difficult, I can focus on getting better rather than only on how I compare with others.
I can judge progress by what I am learning or improving, not only by how I perform compared with others.
I can pursue strong performance without needing my results to prove that I am better than other people.
I can want to do well without needing to prove that I am better than classmates.
I can value strong performance without relying on comparison with others to judge my personal worth.
When a task makes me worry about failing or looking incompetent, I can still choose to engage with it.
I can take on a task even when I'm worried it might make me look less capable than others.
When a goal is no longer realistic or useful, I can consider what has changed before deciding whether to continue pursuing it.
If circumstances change, I can decide whether I need to change my plan, my goal or both.
When circumstances or evidence change, I can reassess whether to continue, change the route or revise the goal.
